title: The Adventures of Haroun-al-Raschid, Caliph of Baghdad
paragraphs: The Caliph Haroun-al-Raschid sat in his palace, wondering whether anything was left in the world that could give him even a few hours of amusement, when his old and trusted friend Giafar, the grand vizier, suddenly appeared before him. Giafar bowed low and waited, as was his duty, for his master to speak. But Haroun-al-Raschid only turned his head to look at him, and sank back into his earlier weary slump.
Giafar, however, had something important to tell the Caliph and had no intention of being put off by silence. So he bowed low again in front of the throne and began to speak.

“Commander of the Faithful,” he said, “I have taken it upon myself to remind your Highness that you have undertaken to observe in secret how justice is done and order is kept throughout the city. Today is the day you set aside for this purpose, and perhaps in carrying out this duty you may find some relief from the melancholy that, to my sorrow, I see has taken hold of you.”
“You are right,” answered the Caliph. “I had forgotten all about it. Go and change your coat, and I will change mine.”

A few moments later they both came back into the hall dressed as foreign merchants, and they slipped through a secret door and out into the open country. From there they turned toward the Euphrates, crossed the river in a small boat, and walked through the part of the town on the far bank, without seeing anything that called for their interference. The Caliph and his vizier were pleased with the peace and good order of the city. They made their way to a bridge that led straight back to the palace, and they had already crossed it when an old blind man stopped them, begging for alms.
The Caliph gave him a coin and started to walk on, but the blind man grabbed his hand and held him tight.
“Kind sir,” he said, “whoever you may be, grant me one more favor. Strike me, I beg you, one blow. I have richly deserved it, and even a harsher punishment.”

The Caliph was very surprised at this request, and he answered gently: “My good man, what you ask is impossible. What use would my charity be if I treated you so badly?” As he spoke, he tried to pull free of the blind beggar’s grip.

“My lord,” the man answered, “forgive my boldness and my insistence. Either take back your money or give me the blow I ask for. I have sworn a solemn oath never to accept anything without being punished for it, and if you knew everything, you would see that the punishment is not even a tenth of what I deserve.”

The Caliph was moved by these words, and perhaps even more by the fact that he had other business to attend to. He gave in and struck the man lightly on the shoulder. Then he went on his way, followed by the blind man’s blessing. When they were out of earshot, he said to the vizier, “There must be something very strange behind that man’s behavior—I would like to find out the reason. Go back to him, tell him who I am, and order him to come to the palace tomorrow, after the hour of evening prayer, without fail.”
So the grand vizier returned to the bridge. He handed the blind beggar a coin and then a blow, gave him the Caliph’s message, and went back to join his master.

They continued toward the palace, but as they crossed a square they came upon a crowd watching a young, well-dressed man who was driving a horse at full speed around the open space. He used his spurs and whip so mercilessly that the animal was covered in foam and blood. The Caliph was astonished at this and asked a passer-by what it meant, but nobody could tell him anything except that the same thing happened every day at the same hour.
He walked on, still puzzled, and for now could only tell the vizier to summon the horseman too, to appear before him at the same hour as the blind man.

The next day, after evening prayer, the Caliph entered the hall, and the vizier followed him with the two men we have spoken of, and a third, who has nothing to do with our story. They all bowed low before the throne. Then the Caliph told them to rise and asked the blind man his name.

“Baba-Abdalla,” said the Caliph, “your way of asking for alms yesterday seemed so strange to me that I almost ordered you on the spot to stop causing such a public scandal. But I have sent for you to ask what made you take such a curious vow. Once I know the reason, I can judge whether you should be allowed to go on with it, because I cannot help thinking it sets a very bad example for others. So tell me the whole truth, and hide nothing.”

These words troubled Baba-Abdalla, and he threw himself down at the Caliph’s feet. Then he rose and answered: “Commander of the Faithful, I humbly beg your pardon for pressing your Highness to do something that seems, on the face of it, to have no meaning. In the eyes of men it may well have none. But I regard it as a small payment for a terrible sin I have committed, and if your Highness will be kind enough to hear my story, you will see that no punishment could atone for my crime.”
